newsitem.title: UK: Pollution raises childhood cancer risk - study.
newsitem.headline: Pollution raises childhood cancer risk - study.

text.p: Children born near sources of industrial pollution such as petroleum refineries and cement works are 20 percent more likely to die of leukaemia or other forms of cancer, British researchers reported on Thursday.

A survey of all children who died of cancer in Britain between 1953 and 1980 -- more than 22,000 -- showed that those who died were much more likely than the general population to have been born within five km (three miles) of a polluting refinery, factory or kiln.

Children born within four km (2.5 miles) of a busy motorway or railway also had a higher risk, epidemiologist George Knox of the University of Birmingham wrote in a report in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.
Knox said the rate varied according to just where the children were born and what kind of industry was involved.

But overall it evened out to a 20 percent higher risk. "If a child was born within five km of a hazard, the risk is increased 20 percent compared with children who did not live within the five-km radius," he said in a telephone interview.
Knox said the work was based on earlier surveys done on the link between childhood cancers and x-rays during pregnancy -- a link that is now well-established.
His team noted cancer rates in children by postal code and laid out a map that showed locations of power plants, refineries, factories and non-suspect industries such as breweries or cotton plants.

They found a clear tendency for cancer cases to be found near furnaces, refineries, car and battery factories, crematoria and power stations although, with a few exceptions, nuclear power plants did not seem to be dangerous.
The two main culprits were plants producing volatile organic chemicals and the process of high-temperature combustion.
Many of the identified risk sites did not employ many people, so Knox rejected the idea that parents were exposed at work. "We came to the conclusion that it (the source) must be diffused," he said.
Knox said it was not just the presence of volatile chemicals in the air that endangered the children, but the way in which they react with other chemicals to form new pollutants.

"For a comprehensive single explanation, we must favour direct exposure of pregnant women or young children to airborne substances diffusing into the surrounding environment," he wrote in the journal report.

Knox said interestingly, plants producing benzene -- well known for its carcinogenic properties -- were not associated with the risk. "Perhaps because of the reputation of benzene they are particular about what escapes," he said.
Knox said his team was now using different techniques and data to see if they get the same results.
